the case, unless it be thought that he was the scribe of the
correction to which the Eusebian scribe affixed the number (see
above, and cf. the first of the ‘doubtful’ examples in Plate II).
At one time I was inclined to think that this was so, on the
ground of the ‘monogram’ in this correction, but further con-
sideration has made me think that this is probably not the
case. Thus it remains uncertain whether Α$^1$ belonged to the
scriptorium or should be regarded as one of the earliest hands
who touched the MS. after it had been ‘issued’. Examples
are given in the second column of Plate II.
*The corrector Α$^4$.* There are only a very few corrections
by this hand. It probably belongs to the fourth century, but
according to Dr. Kenyon’s judgement might possibly be a little
later than the scribes hitherto mentioned. It is marked by an
extreme regularity and neatness (see the fourth column of
Plate II).
*The corrector Α$^5$.* This scribe, easily distinguished by his
graceful style, and the curious shape of his <term>ξ</term>, only made a few
corrections. He is no doubt contemporary with the MS. or
nearly so, but there is nothing to show whether he did or
did not belong to the scriptorium. Examples are given in
the third column of Plate II.
*Α$^{Herm}$.* Possibly distinct from all the other Α correctors is
one who seems to have acted as the <term>διορθωτής (διορθωτής)</term> of Hermas in
a small delicate hand. Examples are given in the third
column of Plate II.
All the scribes hitherto dealt with belong to the Α group
which Tischendorf regarded as belonging to the scriptorium.
In some places he expressed himself in such a way as to
give the impression that he meant Α—the $\aleph$ of the critical
Greek Testament—to refer to a single scribe. This he cer-
tainly did not really think, and he only omitted to define the
facts more clearly because it is so often impossible to say to
which of the group any given correction belongs, even though
it is plain that it is not to be assigned to any later hand.
Outside the pure Α family come the scribes known as
Α$^{obliq}$, Β, and Β$^a$. They differ from those which have been
already treated in that they probably do not belong to the
scriptorium. They are, however, not much later than the

---

## Column 2

Α group—the fifth century is the latest date to which they can
be assigned—and they may be regarded as representing the
corrections of some of the earliest owners of the Codex.
*The corrector Α$^{obliq}$.* This scribe, who, as his title suggests,
used sloping characters, is quite unimportant. He only made
a few casual alterations; Tischendorf only classed him in the
Α group because his is a clearly early hand, and he used ink
which is indistinguishable from that of the Α correctors.
Specimens of his script can be seen in the fourth column of
Plate II.
*The corrector B.* Far more interest attaches to the work
of this scribe, whose writing is chiefly distinguishable from the
Α group by a slight difference of tint, which is not discernible
in a photograph. He was contemporary with the Α group
or nearly so, and was chiefly interested in small points of
spelling and scholarship. On the first pages of Matthew he
made frequent corrections which are very important for the
history of the orthographical tradition as to proper names,
but his interest soon declined, and his hand is not found
outside the first Gospel. He may very well have been a
scholarly owner, who had strong opinions as to the proper
way of spelling the names of the Patriarchs and Kings of
Israel. Tischendorf gives a full list of the corrections; it is
exceedingly difficult to see them either in the facsimile or in
the MS., but there is not, I believe, any reason for doubting
the correctness of his judgement. With great trouble I suc-
ceeded in verifying in the MS. all the corrections which
Tischendorf indicates on f. 1. So far as I can judge the
facsimile is not more obscure than the MS., except in so far as
in a MS. the sense of touch often helps to detect erasures, or
the erosions of faded ink, and this is of course impossible in
a photographic facsimile. It may, however, be thought with
some probability that the MS. was in a better condition when
Tischendorf first saw it than now. The Imperial Library at
St. Petersburg is no doubt in every other respect an infinitely
better home for a MS. than the convent of St. Catherine, but
on the important matter of climate one may suspect that the
advantage is with Sinai. Specimens of B are given in the
third column of Plate II.
*The corrector Β$^a$.* This symbol was used by Tischendorf to
indicate a few corrections in a hand which cannot with cer-
tainty be identified either with B or with any of the Α group.

Eusebian section numbers with canon indicators (e.g., Section ΤΛΑ / Α) are present in the margins. Standard Nomina Sacra like ΙΣ, ΘΣ, and ΑΝΟΣ are expanded. Note the marginal correction in Col 1 for "λεγόμενον" and liturgical notes above Col 3.</meta>

<meta>This page from the Codex Sinaiticus (4th century CE) contains the Gospel of Mark from 2:19 to 3:21 across four columns. The text is in Greek uncials, transcribed here in modern polytonic Greek. Notable features include several Nomina Sacra (ΘΥ, ΑΝΟΣ, ΙΣ) and marginal Eusebian section numbers (ΚΑ-ΚΗ). There are also corrections by later hands, notably an insertion of "Ἰδουμαίας" in Mark 3:8 and small crosses marking paragraph breaks.</meta>

<meta>This folio contains the conclusion of the Gospel of Mark (16:2–8) and the beginning of the Gospel of Luke (1:1–17). Notably, the Codex Sinaiticus omits the "longer ending" of Mark (16:9–20), ending the book at 16:8 followed by a decorative colophon. The text is written in four columns. Marginal notations include Eusebian section and canon numbers for Mark. A later hand has added a Greek note in the blank space of the second column.</meta>

Notable passages include the Parable of the Good Samaritan (Col 2), Jesus visiting Martha and Mary (Col 3), and the Lord's Prayer (Col 4). Significant later corrections are visible, including the restoration of verse 32 (the Levite) in the bottom margin of Column 2 and an expansion of the Lord's Prayer in Column 4.</meta>

<meta>This page contains the conclusion of the Gospel of Luke (24:23–53). It is formatted in four columns of Greek uncial script. Notable features include several later corrections (corrector group C), specifically the addition of Luke 24:51b "καὶ ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν" in the top margin of the fourth column, and "καὶ ἐπέγνωσαν αὐτόν" in the second column. The text ends with a decorative subscriptio identifying the book as the Gospel according to Luke.</meta>

<meta>This page contains the beginning of the Gospel of John (John 1:1–38). The text is written in four columns. The script is Greek uncial (scriptio continua), which has been segmented into words and transcribed into polytonic Greek. It includes Eusebian section numbers in the margins and several nomina sacra. Note that in John 1:18 (Column 2, line 40), the manuscript famously reads "μονογενὴς θεός" instead of "μονογενὴς υἱός".</meta>

<meta>John 5:37–6:23. This folio (250 recto) contains four columns of Greek uncial script. It covers the end of Jesus' testimony in Jerusalem and the beginning of the signs in Galilee (Feeding of the 5,000 and Walking on Water). Marginal section numbers (Eusebian canons) are present (45-53). Notable corrections by later hands (S1/S2) include an addition in the margin of Column 3 related to the distribution of bread and a correction in the margin of Column 4.</meta>

<meta>John 8:41 - 9:14. This page contains four columns of Greek uncial script. It covers the conclusion of Jesus' discourse with the Jews in the temple and the healing of the man born blind. Eusebian section numbers (90-100) are marked in the margins. A significant textual variant is found at the top of the page: a later corrector added the longer ending of John 8:59 ("καὶ διελθὼν διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν ἐπορεύετο καὶ παρῆγεν οὕτως"), which is absent from the original hand of the manuscript.</meta>

<note>Correction for John 8:59 in top margin:</note>
-> καὶ διελθὼν διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν ἐπορεύετο <-
-> καὶ παρῆγεν οὕτως <-

It covers the end of chapter 6 regarding sexual immorality and the body as a temple, and the beginning of chapter 7 regarding marriage and status. Notable features include a later correction in column 2 adding the phrase "fasting and" to the instruction on prayer, and several nomina sacra.</meta>

<header>ΠΡΟΣ ΘΕΣΣΑΛΟΝΙΚΕΙΣ Β / ΠΡΟΣ ΕΒΡΑΙΟΥΣ</header>
<meta>This page contains the conclusion of the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians (2:17-3:18) and the beginning of the Epistle to the Hebrews (1:1-13). It features 4 columns of Greek uncial script. Notable features include a decorative colophon for 2 Thessalonians and a stichometric note (180 lines) before the title of Hebrews. There are minor interlinear corrections, particularly in Column 2.</meta>

It documents the final moments of Stephen's martyrdom, the subsequent persecution of the church led by Saul, the flight of the believers into Judea and Samaria, Philip's ministry in Samaria, and the encounter with Simon the sorcerer. A marginal note in a later hand is visible in Column 1.</meta>

<header>ΒΑΡΝΑΒΑ ΕΠΙΣΤΟΛΗ</header>
<meta>This page marks the transition between the New Testament and the Apostolic Fathers in the Codex Sinaiticus. Column 1 contains the conclusion of the Book of Revelation (Apocalypse of John) 22:19-21, followed by a decorative subscription. Columns 2, 3, and 4 contain the beginning of the Epistle of Barnabas (Barnabas 1:1 - 2:6). The text is written in four columns. Notable features include a decorative title frame for the end of Revelation and occasional marginal numbers.</meta>

The scribe uses scriptio continua, which has been segmented here into modern polytonic Greek for readability. Notable features include the use of nomina sacra (abbreviated sacred names with overlines) and various marginal corrections and notes.
